unit.title: Indices and benchmarks
unit.description: What each index measures, how it's weighted and how to use it to measure your returns

u7l2.title: S&P 500, Nasdaq, IBEX 35 and MSCI World

texts: Spread across the planet
Leo
I've got an MSCI World fund: I'm spread across the whole planet.
What do you tell Leo?
Yes: every country equally
No: over two thirds is the US and there are no emerging markets.
Very diversified, but mostly in the US
Exactly. Over a thousand companies, but not spread out evenly.
It mainly depends on Europe
Europe weighs much less: what moves it most is the US.
So how do I know what's inside each index?
Look at its breakdown by country and sector. The name isn't enough.
Is it in the MSCI World?
The **MSCI World** brings together large and mid-sized companies from **23 developed countries**. Which of these are in it?
It's in
Out: emerging country
Apple (US)
The US is developed and makes up over two thirds of the index.
Nestlé (Switzerland)
Switzerland is a developed country: it's in.
Toyota (Japan)
Japan is developed: it's in.
A big Chinese company
China is emerging: it's in the **MSCI ACWI**, not the World.
A big Indian tech company
India is emerging: it's out of the MSCI World.
Inditex (Spain)
Spain is a developed country: Inditex is in.
Sort the six companies.
«Global» doesn't mean spread out: **over two thirds is the US** and there are no emerging markets like China or India. To add them, there's the **MSCI ACWI**.
Hint: China, India and Brazil are emerging countries.
Over a thousand companies, but not from every country.
Tap each company: in or out?

steps.title: The big indices
steps.body:
• **S&P 500:** around 500 large US companies, weighted by market capitalisation; it covers roughly 80 % of the value of the US stock market.
• **Nasdaq 100:** the 100 largest non-financial companies on the Nasdaq; lots of tech.
• **Dow Jones:** just 30 companies; weighted by price.
• **Euro Stoxx 50:** 50 big eurozone companies. **DAX:** Germany.
• **MSCI World:** around 1,250-1,300 companies in 2026; the figure changes with each review.
steps.key: Each index measures one part of the market: look at what's inside before comparing yourself with it.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, compare the S&P 500 chart with the IBEX 35 chart.

texts: The three-company index
Sara
Today almost every company in my S&P 500 fund went down.
And yet the fund went up. How can that be?
A toy index with three companies: A is worth 600 million; B, 300; C, 100. A rises 10 % and the others don't move.
If it weights each company by what it's worth, how much does the index rise?
The same as A
A weighs 600 out of 1,000, **60 %**: the index rises 6 %.
Quite a lot, but less than A
Exactly. A weighs 60 %: the index rises 6 %.
A third of A's rise: it's one of three
That would be if they weighed the same. A weighs 60 %: it rises 6 %.
So the big ones call the shots.
**Market cap = price × number of shares.** The most valuable one weighs most.
How is each index weighted?
Almost all modern indices weight each company by what it's **worth on the market**. Some don't.
By market cap
By price
All equal
By market cap: the biggest weigh most.
Dow Jones
By share price: an old-fashioned method.
IBEX 35
By market cap, counting only freely traded shares.
Nikkei 225
Also by price, like the Dow Jones.
MSCI World
By market cap: that's why the US weighs so much.
An equal-weighted index
They all weigh the same, big or small.
Sort the six indices.
In a **price-weighted** index, the share with the highest unit price weighs most, even if the company is smaller. That's why almost all of them use **market cap**.
Hint: only the Dow Jones and the Nikkei 225 go by price.
A share's price doesn't tell you how big the company is.
Tap each index: how is it weighted?

steps.title: Concentration
steps.body: With market-cap weighting, the winners weigh more and more. In 2026, a handful of tech companies make up more than a third of the S&P 500: buying the index largely means buying those companies. Look at its top 10 holdings: they tell you what you're really buying.
steps.key: Market cap = price × number of shares; the more it's worth, the more it weighs.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, compare how much Apple moves today with the S&P 500.

u7l4.title: Price index and total return index

texts: The IBEX that «didn't go up»
Real data: **€10,000** in the IBEX 35 at the end of 2006, the index you see in the news. Hit «Start».
Make it to the end, whether you sell or not.

On monthly closes, the IBEX price index didn't beat its 2007 high **until October 2025**, and €10,000 was €12,235 at the end of 2025. But it doesn't count dividends: **the IBEX 35 with dividends has been well above it**.
You've sold. Watch what happens next…
Down by more than half. And that's without dividends.
Down 20 %… and this index doesn't count dividends.
Hit «Start». You can sell whenever you like
With or without dividends
That IBEX is a **price index**: it doesn't count dividends. Imagine one whose price rises 5 % a year and that pays out another 2 % in dividends.
Over 30 years, how much difference does reinvesting that 2 % in dividends make?
Almost none: 2 % is small
Some: 10 % more
Almost double the money
Raise the return to 7 %: price plus reinvested dividends.

**Total return** indices, such as the IBEX 35 with dividends, assume they're reinvested: **over 30 years, almost double**. These are examples, not promises: indices don't rise by the same amount every year.
That's reinvesting dividends: look at the difference.
Stretch the years: the difference compounds.
Raise the return from 5 % to 7 %

steps.title: Compare like with like
steps.body:
If you count the dividends you receive, compare yourself with the index **with dividends**. If not, it'll look like you're doing better than you are.

An **accumulating fund** reinvests the dividends for you.
steps.key: To measure a long-term investment, use the index with dividends.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, look for an ETF with «Acc» in its name: it reinvests dividends.

texts: «I made money»
Pablo
This year my portfolio of Spanish shares made 4 %. Nice!
That year, the IBEX 35 with dividends rose 12 %.
What do you tell Pablo?
Great: a gain is a gain
Making less than the simplest alternative is also losing.
He came in 8 points behind his benchmark
Exactly. An IBEX index fund would have given him three times as much.
Compare himself with a deposit at 2 %
That's a different risk: shares get compared with a share index.
Oh… so how do I compare myself properly?
Same period, same currency, with dividends and after fees.
Which index do you compare yourself with?
Your **benchmark** index has to resemble what you invest in. And always with dividends.
MSCI World
IBEX 35
A portfolio of shares from across the developed world
Large and mid-sized companies from 23 developed countries: the MSCI World.
Shares in Santander, Iberdrola and Inditex
Big Spanish companies: the IBEX 35 with dividends.
A fund of large US companies
Around 500 large US companies: the S&P 500 with dividends.
A fund with Apple, Nestlé, Toyota and over a thousand companies
Lots of developed countries at once: the MSCI World.
A fund of large Spanish companies
The Spanish stock market: the IBEX 35 with dividends.
Shares in Apple, Microsoft and Amazon
Big US companies: the S&P 500 with dividends.
Find the benchmark for the six portfolios.
The benchmark has to **resemble your portfolio**: global with the MSCI World, Spanish with the IBEX 35 and US with the S&P 500, always **with dividends**.
Hint: look at which country the companies are from.
Comparing yourself with something unlike your portfolio tells you nothing.
Tap each portfolio: which index do you compare it with?
Falling behind compounds too
Two funds in the same market return 7 % gross. One costs 0.2 % a year; the other, 1.8 %: **1.6 points behind** every year.
With €10,000 over 30 years, how much of the result do those 1.6 points eat up?
1.6 %, not much
Just over a third
Almost all of it
The cheap one ends up at **€71,968** and the expensive one at **€45,759**: €26,209 lost, 36 %.
Take the timeframe to 30 years.

Beating the index is hard even for professionals: according to SPIVA (end of 2025), **97 %** of active European equity funds lagged it over 10 years. And the average investor earns **1.2 points a year less** than their funds by buying and selling at the wrong time (Morningstar). Try it: find the index in Market that looks like your portfolio and add it to your Favourites.
Over a third, just from falling behind every year.
Keep going: the points you lose compound too.
Stretch the years and watch the difference

u7l2-1.prompt: Match each index with what it measures.
u7l2-1.explanation: Each index is a different window onto the market.
right: The 100 largest non-financials on the Nasdaq
Large and mid caps from 23 developed countries

u7l2-2.prompt: Real daily candlesticks from one of the indices in this lesson, with no name or dates. Does it go up or down over the next sessions?
u7l2-2.explanation: Nobody can reliably read two weeks of an index: that's why indices are benchmarks, not crystal balls.

u7l2-3.prompt: Which index also includes emerging markets such as China or India?
u7l2-3.explanation: The MSCI World only includes developed countries; the ACWI adds emerging markets.

options: How the Spanish stock market is doing
How developed countries are doing as a whole
A fund with Apple, Nestlé, Toyota and over a thousand other companies
How large US companies are doing
A fund of large Spanish companies
u7l2-6.explanation: Always pick the index that resembles what you're looking at.

u7l2-8.prompt: Nasdaq 100, March 2000: tech has been soaring for years and everyone's talking about the internet. What did the index do over the following years?
u7l2-8.explanation: An index heavily concentrated in one sector depends on what happens to that sector, for better and for worse.

u7l2-10.prompt: The MSCI World covers large and mid-sized companies from ____ developed countries.
u7l2-10.explanation: 23 developed countries; for emerging markets there's the MSCI Emerging Markets and, combined, the ACWI.

u7l3-5.prompt: In a price-weighted index, such as the Dow Jones, what weighs most?
options: The share with the highest price per share
The company worth most on the stock market
The one with the most employees
u7l3-5.explanation: That's why it's not a very logical method: a share's price doesn't tell you how big the company is.

u7l3-7.prompt: A €500 share always belongs to a bigger company than a €50 share.
u7l3-7.explanation: It depends on the number of shares: what counts is price × number of shares.

u7l3-8.prompt: Company X: 100 million shares at €50. Company Y: 1,000 million at €10. Which weighs more in a cap-weighted index?
u7l3-8.explanation: X is worth €5,000 million; Y, €10,000 million. Y weighs twice as much even though its share is cheaper.

u7l3-11.prompt: Laura buys an S&P 500 fund thinking it has «500 companies in equal parts». What should she do?
u7l3-11.explanation: Understanding how an index is weighted means knowing what risk you're buying.
feedback: In reality the big ones weigh far more: her risk depends on a few companies.
It isn't badly built: that's how market-cap weighting works. She just needs to understand it.
She finds out a handful of tech companies weigh more than a third: now she knows what she's really buying.

u7l4-4.prompt: What does a total return index measure?
u7l4-4.explanation: It's what an investor who reinvested everything would have made.

u7l4-6.prompt: Nikkei 225 (Japan), December 1989: the index has had years of spectacular gains. What did it do over the following years?
u7l4-6.explanation: You can see what happened on the chart. Remember it's a price index: it doesn't count the dividends its holders received.

u7l4-7.prompt: Match each term with its meaning.
u7l4-7.explanation: To compare properly, always compare «with dividends» with «with dividends».
right: Part of the profit that's paid out
Just the change in share prices

u7l4-8.prompt: What do you say to Lumi?
options: That IBEX doesn't count dividends; with them, it's a very different story
He's right, it doesn't pay anything
u7l4-8.explanation: The price index only tells half the story.
feedback: That's it! The IBEX 35 with dividends has been way above the price index.
He's missing one part: the dividends.
It's calculated correctly: it just measures something else, the price.
lines: My uncle says that for years the IBEX didn't go up at all from 2007 🤷
So the Spanish stock market doesn't pay anything?

u7l4-10.prompt: You compare your portfolio, counting the dividends you received, with the IBEX 35 price index. What happens?
options: You're giving yourself an advantage: you should use the IBEX with dividends
You're putting yourself at a disadvantage
u7l4-10.explanation: You count dividends and the index doesn't: it'll look like you're doing better than you are.

u7l5-6.prompt: Marta picks a fund because it beat its index last year. What should she do?
options: Pick the one that lost most to «buy cheap»
Invest everything: if it won, it'll win again
Also look at its 5-10 year track record and its costs
u7l5-6.explanation: Past success doesn't predict the future: look at long periods and costs.
feedback: Losing a lot one year doesn't mean it'll win the next either.
According to SPIVA, very few funds that beat the index in one period do it again in the next.
She checks whether it was one year's luck or something consistent, and how much it costs.

u7l5-7.prompt: According to SPIVA (end of 2025), what percentage of active European equity funds lagged their index over 10 years?
u7l5-7.explanation: Almost all of them: costs and competition make beating the index for years very hard.

u7l5-10.prompt: Comparing an equity portfolio with a deposit at 2 % is a good way to tell whether you're managing it well.
u7l5-10.explanation: They're different risks. An equity portfolio is compared with a similar equity index.

u7l3-12.prompt: What do you say to Lumi?
options: Yes: they're just a few companies out of 500
It doesn't notice at all: the fund is diversified
It notices quite a lot: by market cap, those few weigh a huge amount
u7l3-12.explanation: Counting companies is misleading («they're just a few out of 500»): in a cap-weighted index each one weighs what it's worth, and those few make up more than a third.
feedback: They're few, but they make up more than a third of the index: if they fall, your fund feels it a lot.
Diversified doesn't mean evenly spread: the big ones call the shots.
That's it! In 2026, a handful of tech companies make up more than a third of the S&P 500.
lines: My S&P 500 fund barely notices if the big tech companies fall, right?

u7l5-11.prompt: What do you say to Lumi?
options: You put part of that in yourself: the real gain is much smaller
u7l5-11.explanation: Looking only at how much the account has grown is misleading. To measure what you earn, subtract what you've contributed: otherwise you're comparing yourself with an advantage.
feedback: Not all of it is profit: you put in €1,000 yourself. What you contribute isn't return.
That's it! You made €300: the rest is money you put in.
Not that either: the portfolio is worth more than everything you put in.
lines: I started the year with €5,000, added €1,000 more and I'm ending it with €6,300

u7l5-12.prompt: Leo has a fund of large US companies. This year his fund went up and the IBEX 35 went down, and Leo boasts: «I'm doing better than the stock market». What do you tell him?
options: That he's right: he beat the IBEX
That he should compare himself with a deposit
That he should compare himself with the S&P 500 with dividends, which looks like his fund
u7l5-12.explanation: Your benchmark has to look like what you invest in. Comparing yourself with whichever index makes you look best is cheating: that way anyone «beats the market».
feedback: Beating an index that doesn't look like your portfolio says nothing about how you're doing.
It's a different risk: shares are compared with a similar share index.
His fund is made of large US companies: that's his yardstick, not the Spanish stock market.
